newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - FEB 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - FEB 24.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The fall in interest rates has transformed past issues of state titles, shares and new multi-year bonds into magnets for investment. With the decision of five state-run banks to drop rates on Friday, investment choices are continually changing.

--The speedier de-escalation of interest rates and handling of foreign exchange policies will lead to forex loans becoming less attractive for the public but there is no intention on the part of the Bank of Greece to take any measures to undercut forex lending, sources say.

--A new justice ministry bill foresees speedier procedures for bankruptcy filers and the prompt satisfaction of creditors. Other clauses foresee the ability to take to court decisions to shut down firms for taxation violations.

--The Latsis Group's Eurobank has recently made an attempt to buy out Zurich's Royal Bank of Scotland, reliable sources say. The buyout was conducted by Luxembourg's Banque de Deports, also owned by the Latsis Group.

--Although there are no thoughts of abolishing the special bank charge EFTE, both the government and the Bank of Greece are examining ways to deal with irregularities in the collection of the charge, sources said over the weekend. The examination of EFTE follows the realilsation by both government and central bank officials that the charge is causing problems and irregularities in the market and the justified complaints of both foreign and domestic banks working in Greece must be dealt with. The changes will lead towards the facilitating of business financing and the creation of more competitive conditions in the domestic banking system.

--State-run banks proceeded to a barrage of reduced lending rates on Friday: smaller banks are expected to follow their lead. However, interest rates continue to be high in comparison to current rates of inflation and when the cost of tax and other charges are calculated. Also worrying is the continued discrepancy between interest rates for lending and deposits.

--The real estate market in Athens and on developed Aegean islands is one of the most expensive in the world, according to a recent survey. Apart from a few exceptions, such as Manhattan, prices for real estate in some of Athens' more exclusive suburbs are way above asking prices for similar or better properties in Europe and the United States.

--Greek and foreign construction companies have taken up battle positions over the share of public works projects with Greek firms filing suit against the Hochtief-led "Athens Airport" consortium and Public Works Minister Costas Laliotis being called on to intervene in the preliminary selection of the 25-billion-drachma Egnatia Highway.

--National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou's plans for the merger of banks to create stronger and fewer groups are based on a study which claims that modernisation and expansion of new banking products and services are the response to new conditions of competitiveness which will prevail until the year 2000. Changes will include structural changes in the operation of banks, with the reduction of operating costs and training of personnel, new and more effective forms of dealing with risk and further strengthening of the capital market.

--The good old days for the food and beverages industry have receded with net profit margins narrowing although major supermaket chains are increasing their profits. One hundred production firms had total sales of one trillion drachmas, as much as the 10 largest supermarket chains.

--The battle over the issue of trading hours has become a war of interests, with the recent agreement coming in for fire by a number of retailers - chief among them Marinopoulos and Continent - fearing a restriction of their turnover and threating price increases and lay-offs.

--The idea of the establishment of a social security bank promoted by the General Confederation of Workers of Greece and major unions led in part to the recent furore over the government's plans to utilise pension funds' reserve capital. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
